prompt: Write a ~700-word piece of literary short fiction about: the last week of a village post office. Prose only, no headings.
text:
The old post office had stood on its corner for as long as anyone could remember, its wooden façade weathered to a soft silver that seemed to glow in the fading light of day. Now, with just six days left before it closed forever, the silence was almost palpable.

Inside, Margaret worked diligently at her desk, stamping letters and sorting packages with a quiet efficiency. It was a job she loved, one that had given her purpose for so many years. But on this final week, even the familiar rhythms of the post office seemed tinged with melancholy. As customers trickled in to collect their mail, their faces seemed to convey not just happiness at receiving letters from far-flung friends and family, but also a reluctant acceptance that something precious was coming to an end.

Mrs. Jenkins, the village gossip, came in on Monday morning, her silver hair styled with extra care for the occasion. She handed Margaret a small package wrapped in brown paper and tied with twine. "This is from my sister in Australia," she said, her voice trembling slightly as she watched the post office's last weeks tick away.

On Tuesday, it was Tom, the young farmer, who came to collect his mail. He was usually gruff and taciturn, but today he smiled hesitantly at Margaret as he handed over a stamp and took his letters in return. "I never thought I'd say this," he said, "but I'm going to miss coming here."

Wednesday brought a visit from the village children, who tumbled into the post office like a miniature parade. They chattered excitedly about their pen pals, whose letters were always filled with stories of distant lands and exotic adventures. As Margaret sorted through the mail, she couldn't help but feel a pang of sadness for these young lives that had grown up alongside her own.

Thursday's customer was Mrs. Ali, who owned the village shop. She came in to pay her rent by cheque, her eyes fixed on the old post office as if it were a living thing about to be extinguished. "I remember when you first opened," she said to Margaret. "My daughter was just born that year."

Friday brought a flurry of activity, as the post office's remaining customers came in to collect their mail before the final closure. The atmosphere inside was almost festive, with people laughing and chatting as they handed over stamps and took their letters in return.

As Margaret locked up at 5 pm on Friday evening, she felt a weight settle onto her shoulders. For so long, this post office had been more than just a place to send mail – it had been the heart of the village. And now, with just one day left before its doors closed forever, even the air seemed heavy with grief.

On Saturday morning, Margaret opened up once more for the final time. As she worked, the silence grew more profound, punctuated only by the occasional rustling of paper or the soft ticking of a clock on the wall. She knew that today would be different from all the others – the last day, in every sense.

As the morning wore on, fewer and fewer customers came to collect their mail. The village children, who had once flocked to the post office like birds, now played instead in the park across the street. Even the air seemed stiller, as if it too were mourning the passing of an era.

Margaret worked diligently until midday, when the last customer left and the silence finally descended. She stood behind her counter for a moment, running her fingers over the familiar surfaces – the stamp machine, the scales, the worn wooden desk where she had spent so many years sorting letters and packages.

Then, with a quiet sense of ritual, she locked up the post office for the very last time. As she walked out into the bright sunlight, Margaret felt the weight on her shoulders shift once more – this time, to a place of acceptance and understanding. For in the village's loss, there was also something beautiful: the knowledge that even as things changed, some moments would remain forever unchanged.

The old post office stood empty for a while longer, its wooden façade still radiating a soft silver glow into the fading light of day. But eventually, like all things that must end, it too came to an end – left behind only memories and the faintest whisper of what once was.
